text.content:
A wanderer’s first steps into the tricksome and beguiling forest.

This Quick-Start is a gateway to adventure in the perilous realm of Dolmenwood—a swathe of tangled woods, fungus-encrusted glades, and foetid marsh on the wild borders of civilisation. Rife with intrigue, secrets, and magic, Dolmenwood draws travellers of adventurous spirit, daring them to venture within.

Required Materials

To experience your first foray into Dolmenwood, you’ll need the following:

  • 1 Referee: The games master who will read this book and run the adventure.
  • 3–6 players: Participants who will each take on the role of an adventurer in Dolmenwood.
  • Polyhedral dice: Dolmenwood uses standard RPG dice, primarily [[/r d4]], [[/r d6]], [[/r d8]], and [[/r d20]].
  • Notebook: Pencils and blank paper for making notes and mapping.

In This Quick-Start

Basic rules: @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.wKXecJ2zBpYbp0YM]{Basic Rules}.

Pre-generated characters: @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.G4cK3x6Ra07C05pg]{Pre-Generated Characters}.

Character abilities: @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.eDNtMfg3bNhBPFll]{Magic}. @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.8FVlwfkh4TTlTdyd]{Skills}.

Adventuring rules: @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.VZf0yjDdzU0n7ACW]{Exploration}. @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.exB7FvXNYZH0tEhr]{Encounters}. @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.U0lHH7E917TC6imv]{Combat}.

The Weaver & the Redcaps adventure: @UUID[JournalEntry.BbGTV9re1UrfASrM.JournalEntryPage.keKzdM7mTyOJ3uW5]{The Weaver & the Redcaps}.

Starting Play

The Referee should read the whole Quick-Start before play, to understand the adventure and the game’s basic rules. Players should look over the available characters (@UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.G4cK3x6Ra07C05pg]{Pre-Generated Characters}) and choose one each, referring to the basic rules guide on @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.wKXecJ2zBpYbp0YM]{Basic Rules} as needed.

Spell casters: Anyone playing Merrild Bockstump or Guillem Dunwaller should choose a spell—see @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.eDNtMfg3bNhBPFll]{Magic}.

Character Advancement

Players aim to advance in the game by earning Experience Points (XP), awarded by the Referee (see @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.VZf0yjDdzU0n7ACW]{Exploration}). XP is primarily awarded for treasure acquired on adventures, plus a small amount for defeating enemies.

Levelling up: The Dolmenwood Player’s Book has full rules for advancing characters up to Level 15.

Dolmenwood Lore

Sentient Folk

While humans dominate the settled reaches of Dolmenwood, they are not the only folk to call the place home.

Breggles: The High Wold region of south-western Dolmenwood has been ruled since ancient times by the goat-headed breggles. Breggles are divided into two castes, distinguished by the length of their horns—aristocratic longhorns and commoner shorthorns.

Mosslings: The dank, fungal-infested lowlands of Mulchgrove, in the eastern woods, are home to a shy and stunted folk called mosslings, part mortal flesh and part plant or fungus.

Fairies and demi-fey: Among the myriad peoples of Fairy, a number venture into Dolmenwood and mingle with mortal folk: elves, otherworldly and beautiful, the little cat-folk known as grimalkins, and bat-faced woodgrues are the most commonly encountered.

Other sentient beings: Off the beaten track, innumerable creatures await discovery. Goblin tricksters peddle fairy fruits and questionable wares; scrabies emerge from their network of tunnels, eager to explore; even a bird or animal may surprise travellers by greeting them from the wayside, spinning a riddle, or cursing their trespass.

Factions and Powers

The Duchy of Brackenwold: Ruling from the supposedly impregnable Castle Brackenwold, the dukes trace their line back to the earliest settlers in the region. All mortal folk within the Wood—from the humblest beggar to the highest lord—pay fealty to the duke.

The Pluritine Church: While it holds much political clout, the monotheistic Pluritine Church is of late diminished in Dolmenwood. Many shrines and chapels dedicated to the hundred saints of the Church have fallen into ruin and been reclaimed by the forest.

Fairy nobles: Where mortals now reign, great fairy nobles once held court. The entirety of Dolmenwood was once the domain of a cruel elf lord known as the Cold Prince, lord of winter eternal. Fearful tales of his return to Dolmenwood and his icy wrath weave a common thread through the folklore of those who dwell within his erstwhile domain.

The Nag-Lord: A wicked, trickster figure of local folklore, said to keep unholy court in the twisted northern woods, where his armies of corrupted breggles and other creatures of Chaos lair. The Nag-Lord is known in folktales as the “King of the Wood,” and is portrayed as being part man, part unicorn, with nine legs.

The most common game rules, including adventurer game statistics.

Dice Rolls

Notation: Dolmenwood uses standard dice rolling notation: “[[/r 2d6+4]]” means roll and sum 2 six-sided dice, then add 4.

Target rolls: Most rules call for a die roll versus a specified target number. Equal or higher succeeds.

Chance rolls: Some rules specify a chance using an X-in-Y notation (e.g. 2-in-6). Roll the appropriate die type (e.g. [[/r d6]] for an X-in-6 chance). Equal to or lower than the specified number means the chance occurs.

Character Statistics

Kindred: Human or another type of fantastic intelligent creature that inhabits Dolmenwood.

Class: An adventuring role or profession.

Level: A character’s expertise as an adventurer. Characters start at Level 1 and advance through successful adventures.

Alignment: Basic moral outlook, determining how certain magic influences a character.

Abilities: Characters are rated with a 3 to 18 score in Strength, Intelligence, Wisdom, Dexterity, Constitution, and Charisma. Associated with each score is a –3 to +3 Ability Modifier, which applies to various actions.

Armour Class (AC): The ability to avoid damage in combat. AC is determined by the character’s armour (AC 10 if unarmoured) plus their Dexterity Modifier.

Hit Points (HP): The ability to avoid dying. When a character is harmed, their current Hit Point total is reduced. If this number reaches 0, the character dies. Rest restores lost HP, up to the character’s maximum: 1 HP for a good night’s rest, [[/r 1d3]] HP for a full day’s rest.

Attack (Att.): The ability to hit foes in combat. Added to Attack Rolls (see below).

Speed: The number of feet a character can move each Round (approximately 10 seconds) in combat.

Magic Resistance (MR): A modifier applied when a character tries to resist harmful magic.

Save Targets: The ability to avoid different types of dangerous or detrimental effects, denoted as a target number to equal or beat on [[/r 1d20]]. There are 5 categories: Doom, Ray, Hold, Blast, Spell (abbreviated D R H B S).

Skill Targets: Skill with specialised adventuring tasks, denoted as a target number to equal or beat on [[/r 1d6]].

Time

Game time is measured in Turns (approximately 10 minutes) when exploring an adventure site and Rounds (approximately 10 seconds) during combat.

Core Game Rules

Ability Checks

Determine whether a character succeeds at a challenging task related to one of their innate Abilities.

Rolling: Roll [[/r 1d6]] and add the Modifier of the Ability being tested. If the result equals or exceeds a target number of 4, the check succeeds

1s and 6s: A roll of natural 1 always fails and a roll of natural 6 always succeeds, irrespective of modifiers.

Attack Rolls

Determine whether an attacker lands a blow.

Rolling: Roll [[/r 1d20]], adding the character’s Attack, plus their Strength Modifier for melee attacks or their Dexterity Modifier for missile attacks. If the result equals or exceeds the defender’s Armour Class, the attack hits. Make a Damage Roll.

1s and 20s: A roll of natural 1 always fails and a roll of natural 20 always succeeds, irrespective of modifiers.

Damage Rolls

Determine the number of Hit Points lost by the target of a successful Attack Roll.

Rolling: Roll the die listed for the weapon used, adding the character’s Strength Modifier for melee attacks.

Unarmed attacks: Punching, kicking, and similar inflicts [[/r 1d2]] damage, plus Strength Modifier.

Saving Throws

Determine whether a character avoids a dangerous or detrimental effect—for example, a banshee’s deadly wail or a wyrm’s acidic breath. There are 5 Save Categories, each rolled for a different type of hazard: Doom, Ray, Hold, Blast, Spell (abbreviated D R H B S).

Rolling: Roll [[/r 1d20]], aiming to equal or exceeds the character’s Save Target for the applicable Save Category.

Magic: For Saving Throws against effects of magical origin, add the character’s Wisdom Modifier.

1s and 20s: A roll of natural 1 always fails and a roll of natural 20 always succeeds, irrespective of modifiers.

Skill Checks

Determine whether a character succeeds at a challenging task related to a specialised adventuring skill. The uses of various skills are described on @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.8FVlwfkh4TTlTdyd]{Skills}.

Rolling: Roll [[/r 1d6]]. If the result equals or exceeds the Skill Target for the skill being tested, the check succeeds

1s and 6s: A roll of natural 1 always fails and a roll of natural 6 always succeeds, irrespective of modifiers.

A selection of six ready-to-play adventurers for players to choose from.

The supernatural abilities of clerics, friars, and magicians.

From the holy blessings of the hundred saints to the tricksome glamours of fairies and the eldritch formulae of magicians, strange powers abound in Dolmenwood.

Line of sight: Unless noted otherwise, a spell’s intended target (a specific creature, object, or area) must be visible to the caster.

Arcane Magic

The workings of magicians, learned by esoteric study and arduous practice.

Memorising spells: After a night’s rest, a magician can spend 1 hour in quiet study to memorise spells from their spell books. A Level 1 magician can memorise one spell from their spell books.

Casting spells: A memorised arcane spell is cast by precisely replicating a specific set of hand gestures and mystical words. When a spell is cast, the imprinted pattern of magical energy is erased from the caster’s mind until memorised again (following a night’s rest).

Freedom: The character must be able to speak and must have one hand free.

Arcane Spells

The spell book Smythe’s Illuminations (possessed by Merrild Bockstump) contains the following spells.

Decipher

For 2 Turns, any script you pass your hand over glows and transforms into the common Woldish tongue. Transformed script reverts when the spell ends.

Ignite / Extinguish

When cast, choose to either ignite or extinguish:

Ignite: A stream of sparks shoots at a target within 30′, either igniting a light source or inflicting 1 damage (the target may Save Versus Ray to avoid).

Extinguish: Whirling zephyrs snuff out a flame (up to the size of a torch) within 30′. If the flame is held by a creature, they may Save Versus Spell to resist.

Ioun Shard

A glowing shard of vividly coloured crystal orbits your head for 2 Turns. At any time you can command it to shoot at a target within 120′. It hits unerringly (no Attack Roll or Saving Throw) and inflicts [[/r 1d6+1]] damage. Once fired, the shard is destroyed.

Holy Magic

The spells bestowed upon devoted adherents of the Pluritine Church.

Praying for spells: After a night’s rest, a holy spell-caster can spend 1 hour in quiet prayer to receive the blessing of a particular saint. A Level 1 friar can pray for one spell, chosen from the list below.

Casting spells: A bestowed holy spell may be cast by reciting a prayer in the Liturgic tongue. When a spell is cast, the saint’s blessing expires until bestowed again.

Speech: The character must be able to speak.

Holy Spells

Breath of St Lillibeth: Lesser Healing

Instantly heals [[/r 1d6+1]] HP to a living creature you touch.

St Benester’s Word: Mantle of Protection

You gain a +1 bonus to AC and Saving Throws when attacked by Chaotic creatures. Creatures created or summoned by magic cannot attack you in melee, unless you attack them. Lasts 12 Turns.

St Foggarty’s Benediction: Light

Conjures a golden radiance, illuminating a 15′ radius area. Lasts 12 Turns.

Wisdom of St Thorm: Detect Magic

Magic within 60′ of you glows. Lasts 2 Turns.

Turning the Undead

Clerics and friars may attempt to drive off undead monsters by presenting their holy symbol and invoking the might of the One True God.

Range: The undead must be within 30′. Concealed undead (e.g. behind doors or in coffers) are unaffected.

Rolling: Roll [[/r 2d6]], subtracting 2 for every Level of the undead monsters above 1. (e.g. subtract 4 for Level 3 undead.) The modified roll determines the effect.

Usage frequency: One attempt per Turn.

Turn Undead Results

RollEffect
4 or lessNone
5–6[[/r 2d4]] undead stunned (unable to act) for 1 Round
7–12[[/r 2d4]] undead flee for 1 Turn

Common adventuring actions and specialised training possessed by some Classes.

Skill Checks are used to determine success with various common adventuring challenges. Only characters with a skill listed on their sheet can attempt it. For example, a thief can attempt Pick Lock, while other characters cannot.

Rolling: @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.wKXecJ2zBpYbp0YM]{See Core Rules}.

Retrying: Unless noted for a specific skill, failed checks can be freely retried.

Referee rolls: The Referee should roll Detect Magic, Listen, and Search Checks on players’ behalf, so that players do not know if the check failed or if there is simply nothing to find.

Alertness

Make an Alertness Check to act normally in a Surprise Round. @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.U0lHH7E917TC6imv]{See Combat}.

Climb Wall

Make a Climb Wall Check to climb vertical or very steep surfaces with only minimal handholds without any special climbing equipment.

Failure: The character makes no progress.

Natural 1: On a roll of natural 1, the character must Save Versus Doom or fall from the half way point, suffering [[/r 1d6]] damage per 10′ of the fall.

Retries: Each subsequent attempt requires 1 Turn.

Easier climbs: Characters with the Climb Wall skill automatically succeed at easier climbs (see @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.VZf0yjDdzU0n7ACW]{Climbing and Falling}), without a roll.

Decipher Document

Make a Decipher Document Check to understand the gist of a non-magical text in a language the character does not speak, unravel a cypher, or identify cryptically labelled landmarks on a map.

No retry: Only once per document.

Detect Magic

Spend 1 Turn and make a Detect Magic Check to attempt to detect enchantments woven into an object, place, or creature being touched.

Disarm Mechanism

Spend 1 Turn using thieves’ tools and make a Disarm Mechanism Check to try to disarm a complex, clockwork-like trap mechanism hidden in a lock, lid, door handle, or similar.

Natural 1: On a roll of natural 1, the character must Save Versus Doom or accidentally spring the trap.

Legerdemain

Make a Legerdemain Check to try to pilfer a small item in the possession of another creature or perform a trick of sleight of hand, such as palming a small object or slipping a poison into a drink.

Difficulty: –1 penalty per three Levels of the victim or observer (e.g. a Level 6 target incurs a –2 penalty).

Natural 1: On a roll of natural 1, the character must Save Versus Doom to avoid being noticed.

Listen

Spend 1 Turn and make a Listen Check to try to hear creatures on the other side of a door.

Pick Lock

Spend 1 Turn using thieves’ tools and make a Pick Lock Check to try to open a lock without the key.

Search

Spend 1 Turn and make a Search Check to search an object or 10′ × 10′ area for hidden features (e.g. traps, secret doors, hidden compartments, etc.).

Stalking

Works the same as Stealth (see below), but only functions in the wilds (i.e. not indoors).

Stealth

Hiding: Make a Stealth Check to remain undetected when shadows are the only cover available. @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.VZf0yjDdzU0n7ACW]{See Hiding and Ambushes}.

Sneaking: If a Surprise Roll indicates the character’s party has been detected, make a Stealth Check to remain undetected. @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.VZf0yjDdzU0n7ACW]{See Sneaking}.

Tracking

Spend 1 Turn and make a Tracking Check to try to find tracks left by creatures in a 30′ × 30′ area in the wilds (i.e. not indoors). If the check succeeds, the character knows the type of creatures that made the tracks and can follow the tracks.

Modifiers: The Referee may specify situational modifiers depending on the conditions, for example: +1 for soft ground, –1 for hard; +1 for tracks made by a group of 10 or more creatures; –2 for active attempts to cover tracks; –1 per day since the tracks were made, –1 per hour of rain or covering snow; –1 for poor lighting.

No retry: Only once per location.

Rules for handling the most common adventuring situations.

Exploration Procedure Per Turn (~10 Minutes)

1. Description: The Referee describes the situation, depicting the environment, any characters, monsters, hazards, or objects present, and noting prominent smells, sounds, etc.

2. Clarification: The players may ask questions of the Referee to clarify any descriptive elements that are unclear to them.

3. Decide actions: The party decides what to do (e.g. moving, searching, listening, entering rooms).

4. Random happenings: The Referee makes a check for random encounters or events (see @UUID[JournalEntry.BbGTV9re1UrfASrM.JournalEntryPage.GlO9vKCRAG0tzRkh]{Cottage Interior}).

5. Description: The Referee describes what happens. If creatures are encountered, follow the procedure described in @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.exB7FvXNYZH0tEhr]{Encounters}.

6. End of Turn: 1 Turn has passed. Keep track of light source and spell durations.

Burning Oil

In addition to their normal use as lantern fuel, oil flasks can be used offensively.

Throwing: A flask can be thrown as a missile attack (range 10′/ 30′/ 50′), soaking a creature on a successful hit. When lit (e.g. by a torch), the oil deals [[/r 1d8]] damage, plus another [[/r 1d8]] damage next combat Round.

Pools: Pouring a flask of oil on the ground creates a 3′ diameter pool. If lit, it burns for 1 Turn. Creatures passing through the flames suffer [[/r 1d8]] damage.

Climbing and Falling

Characters can make trivial climbs in non-pressured situations without a roll (e.g. climbing into the lower branches of a tree). In more difficult or tense situations, the Referee may require a Dexterity Check. If the check fails, the character falls at the halfway point, suffering [[/r 1d6]] damage per 10′ of the fall.

Darkness and Blindness

Wise characters carry illumination—magical or mundane—when exploring at night or underground. Typical light sources enable normal vision within a 30′ radius.

Low light: In low light conditions (e.g. at night without a light source), characters suffer a –2 penalty to Attack Rolls and move at half Speed.

Pitch darkness or blindness: Characters plunged into darkness or suddenly blinded suffer a –4 penalty to Attack Rolls, Armour Class, and Saving Throws and have Speed 10.

Doors

Doors are a common obstacle in dungeons and indoor spaces, restricting vision and access. Furthermore, doors may be locked or hidden from plain sight.

Secret Doors

Whether cunningly integrated into stonework or concealed beneath a blanket of moss, some doors cannot be seen by casual observation. Searching for secret doors is discussed under @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.VZf0yjDdzU0n7ACW]{Hidden Features}.

Locked Doors

If the correct key cannot be located, a locked door may be opened by magic (e.g. a mossling’s lock singing ability), picked by a thief, or broken open.

Breaking open: A successful Strength Check, the use of a tool (e.g. an axe or a crowbar), and 1 Turn of effort are usually enough to smash or pry open a typical wooden door. At the Referee’s discretion, the noise produced may trigger an additional check for random happenings (see @UUID[JournalEntry.BbGTV9re1UrfASrM.JournalEntryPage.GlO9vKCRAG0tzRkh]{Cottage Interior}).

Listening at Doors

Most doors do not block obvious, loud noises. Characters may attempt to detect the presence of creatures waiting quietly beyond a closed door by pressing an ear against it to listen. The Referee then rolls a Listen Check (see @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.8FVlwfkh4TTlTdyd]{Skills}).

Multiple characters: If space permits, multiple characters may listen at the same door. Up to 2 characters can simultaneously listen at a typical door.

Silent monsters: Some monsters (e.g. undead) cannot be detected by listening.

Experience Points (Xp)

After an adventure, the Referee awards XP to the party, based on the following factors:

Treasure: The party gains 1 XP per 1 gold piece value of treasure recovered.

Foes defeated: The party gains XP for every foe defeated (i.e. slain, outsmarted, captured, scared away, etc.). The XP award for a creature is listed in its stat block.

Dividing Party XP

All XP awarded to the party is divided evenly between all party members who survived the adventure.

Hidden Features

Hidden features can often be located simply by describing characters’ actions—for example, a character might lift a rug and reveal a hidden trapdoor. Alternatively, players may declare that they are searching a certain object or 10′ × 10′ area for hidden features (e.g. traps, secret doors, hidden compartments, etc.). The Referee rolls a Search Check.

Time: Each search takes 1 Turn.

Multiple characters: If space permits, multiple characters may search the same object or area. Up to 3 characters can simultaneously search a 10′ × 10′ area.

Retrying: Characters may search the same object or area again as often as they wish, each attempt requiring an additional Turn.

Jumping

Long jumps: Characters can jump across a stream, chasm, or pit of up to 5′ wide with a 20′ run-up—no roll is required. For longer jumps of up to 10′, a Strength Check is required.

High jumps: Characters can jump over obstacles of up to 3′ high with a 20′ run-up—no roll is required. For higher jumps of up to 5′, a Strength Check is required.

Modifiers: –1 if wearing Medium armour (e.g. chainmail), –2 if wearing Heavy armour (e.g. plate mail).

Movement

Characters move at exploration speed: 3 times their Speed in feet each Turn (or up to 10 times their Speed through previously explored, fully mapped areas).

This rate of movement is careful and stealthy, and does not automatically give away a group’s presence. Heavily laden characters must move especially slowly, to avoid armour or other gear making noise. This is factored into characters’ Speed.

Narrative Interaction

The basic exploration procedure is the fundamental means of interacting with the imagined world of the game. The Referee describes the environment, players ask clarifying questions, then characters act and the Referee judges what happens. Sometimes a die roll is required—putting a character’s fate in the hands of chance—but it is often possible to bypass hazards using ingenuity, without any kind of random roll.

Example: Exploring a cave system of crystal-encrusted grottoes, the party comes across a 10′ wide chasm blocking their path. The players ask the Referee if they can jump across. Consulting the rules for jumping, the Referee says that a Strength Check is required. Not liking the odds, the players discuss other approaches. Could the large statue they previously encountered be dragged here and tipped across the chasm as a bridge? Could they attach a rope and grappling hook to rocks on the other side and swing across?

Stealth

When two groups approach each other, there is a chance that one or both is unaware of the other’s presence. This is handled by a Surprise Roll (see @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.exB7FvXNYZH0tEhr]{Encounters}).

Sneaking

When attempting to sneak up on or sneak past a creature, a Surprise Roll is made each Round. If the roll indicates surprise, the sneaking party may move for 1 Round without being detected. Otherwise, the sneaking party is spotted.

Vigilance: If creatures are actively watching (e.g. a guard staring fixedly down a corridor, without moving), the Referee may rule that sneaking is impossible. Most creatures cannot maintain this level of vigilance for long.

Distractions: If creatures are engaged in some activity (e.g. feeding, conversation) or distracted by a noise elsewhere, the Referee may rule that their chance of being surprised is increased.

Lone characters: Sometimes a single character (e.g. a thief or hunter) splits off from the main party to scout ahead. In this case, treat the character as a separate party with their own Surprise Rolls.

Hiding and Ambushes

A common tactic is to hide behind some kind of cover in order to evade detection or to surprise foes. The chance of being spotted by casual passersby is determined by the density of cover available, as judged by the Referee.

Complete cover: A creature fully concealed from view (e.g. behind a wall, inside a closet, etc.) automatically goes undetected.

Partial cover: The Referee should judge the chance of the creature being spotted based on the density of cover, for example as an X-in-6 roll.

Searching: The above assumes enemies casually wandering past the location where a creature is hidden. If an enemy is actively searching, it is only a matter of time before the hiding place is uncovered.

Ambushing: When creatures attack from hiding, the opposing side’s chance of being surprised is increased by 1. For example, the standard 2-in-6 chance of being surprised increases to 3-in-6.

Example: Hearing the echoing footsteps of castle guards approaching, a gang of burglars quickly dives behind cover. One character jumps inside a closet and shuts the door, another hides behind a curtain, and the third crouches behind a statue in a corner. The Referee rules that the character in the closet automatically goes undetected, the character behind the curtain has a 1-in-6 chance of being spotted (their feet are sticking out at the bottom), and the character behind the statue has a 3-in-6 chance.

When adventurers meet strangers, foes, or monsters in the wilds.

Encounter Sequence

1. Awareness: The Referee establishes whether either side is already aware of the other.

2. Surprise: The Referee makes a Surprise Roll, if applicable.

3. Encounter distance: The Referee determines the distance between the two sides.

4. Initiative: Any sides that are not surprised roll [[/r 1d6]] to determine which side acts first. Highest acts first. Both sides act simultaneously on a tie.

5. Actions: Any sides that are not surprised decide how they will respond to the encounter. The encounter is played out accordingly.

6. Conclusion: One Turn has passed.

Sides

Typically there are two sides in an encounter—a PC adventuring party and a group of NPCs or monsters. It is possible to have more than two sides in situations where multiple independent groups meet.

Awareness

Sometimes one group is already aware of the other’s presence, negating the chance of being surprised. The Referee should judge this based on the situation—e.g. a group making a lot of noise or carrying a light in the dark usually makes its presence known to others at some distance.

Surprise

A Surprise Roll is made for any side that is not already aware of the other’s presence. @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.VZf0yjDdzU0n7ACW]{See Stealth} for more details on avoiding detection.

Surprise Rolls: Each side unaware of the other’s presence rolls to see if they are surprised. One player rolls for the adventuring party as a whole, and the Referee rolls for each other side.

Chance of being surprised: The standard chance of a side being surprised is 2-in-6. This may be modified in certain situations. For example, attacking from hiding (see @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.VZf0yjDdzU0n7ACW]{Stealth}) increases the chance of the opposing side being surprised by 1, to 3-in-6.

Effects of Surprise

Neither side surprised: Neither side has an advantage.

One side surprised: The unsurprised side gains a 1 Round advantage, during which the surprised side cannot act.

Both sides surprised: There is simply a momentary confusion—neither side has any advantage.

Monster and NPC Reactions

Circumstances often make it obvious how a monster or NPC will react upon encountering adventurers. If unsure, the Referee may roll [[/r 2d6]] on the table below.

Charisma: When parleying, the Charisma Modifier of the speaking PC is applied to Reaction Rolls.

Encounter Reactions

[[/r 2d6]]Reaction
2 or lessAttacks
3–5Hostile, may attack
6–8Uncertain, wary
9–11Indifferent, may negotiate
12 or moreEager, friendly

Actions

The players decide their actions and the Referee determines other sides’ actions (see Monster and NPC Reactions). The following actions are common.

Attacking

If a side attacks, casts spells, or makes tactical movement, follow the procedure under @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.U0lHH7E917TC6imv]{Combat}. Use the rolled initiative for the first Round of combat, re-rolling in the second and subsequent Rounds.

Evasion

If a side wishes to avoid an encounter, it may try to flee. The opposing side decides whether or not to pursue.

Surprise: If not obviously visible, a side with surprise may avoid the encounter altogether by turning back, waiting quietly, or attempting to sneak past.

Pursuit: If the opposing side decides to gives chase, it is assumed that both sides are running—moving at 3 times their Speed in feet per Round. Game time proceeds in Rounds, with the location of the two sides carefully tracked to determine their relative positions.

Parley

A side may attempt to communicate with the other. If PCs begin an encounter with an attempt to parley, the Charisma of the speaking character can influence the other side’s reaction. See Monster and NPC Reactions.

Waiting

A side may decide to wait to see how the other side acts, essentially forfeiting any element of surprise or initiative it may have had.

When swords are drawn and an encounter turns to violence.

Combat Procedure Per Round (~10 Seconds)

1. Declarations: The intent to cast a spell or retreat from melee must be declared.

2. Initiative: Each side rolls [[/r 1d6]] to determine which side acts first. Highest acts first. Both sides act simultaneously on a tie.

3. Winning side acts: Actions of combatants on the winning side are handled in the following sequence: a. Movement: Combatants may not move when casting a spell. b. Missile attacks: Fired or thrown attacks. c. Magic: Casting spells, using magic items, turning the undead. d. Melee attacks: And other actions.

4. Other sides act: Repeat steps 3a to 3d for each side, in order of initiative (highest first).

5. Morale: The Referee makes a Morale Check for monsters and NPCs, if applicable.

In Melee

Two combatants are treated as being in melee if they are positioned within 5′ and one or both has made a melee attack against the other.

Actions per Round

Combatants may move and perform one action each Round. The following count as a combatant’s action for the Round. For other actions, the Referee must judge what is feasible within the space of a Round.

  • Make an attack.
  • Cast a spell.
  • Drink a potion.
  • Activate a magic item.

The Referee may allow combatants to take momentary actions (e.g. shouting a few words, dropping a held object) in addition to their main action for the Round.

Movement

When in Melee

Combatants can move up to half their Speed in feet per Round.

Fleeing from melee: A combatant wishing to move at greater than half Speed must turn and flee melee, forfeiting their attack this Round. Opponents in melee with a retreating combatant gain a +2 Attack bonus against them this Round and ignore any AC bonus from their shield.

Outside of Melee

Combatants can move up to their Speed in feet per Round.

Fleeing an encounter: Combatants not in melee may flee a combat encounter, beginning running movement (3 times Speed in feet per Round).

Attacking

Melee attacks are possible when opponents are 5′ or less from each other. Missile attacks are possible when opponents are more than 5′ from one another. @UUID[JournalEntry.Zsu4G7vJJBdnuJIs.JournalEntryPage.wKXecJ2zBpYbp0YM]{See Attack Rolls}.

Number of attacks: Player Characters can make one attack per Round. Some monsters can make multiple attacks each Round, as listed in their stat block.

Rear attacks: Negate AC bonuses from shields.

Missile range: Missile weapons are listed with 3 range bands, which determine an Attack modifier: Short: +1, Medium: +0, Long: –1. Beyond Long: cannot attack.

Missile cover: The Referee may apply Attack Roll penalties of between –1 and –4 if a target is hiding behind partial cover. For example, a small table might incur a –1 penalty, dense woods might incur a –4 penalty. Targets behind full cover cannot be hit.

Casting Spells in Combat

Movement: Characters casting a spell cannot move in the same Round.

Disruption: If a character casting a spell is successfully attacked or fails a Saving Throw before their side’s initiative, the spell is disrupted and fizzles out with no effect (erased from the caster’s memory).

Morale

If a battle is going against them, combatants may decide to retreat, flee, or surrender. Players always make this decision for their characters, but the Referee may roll to determine if monsters or NPCs break morale.

Morale Checks: Roll [[/r 2d6]]. If the result exceeds the combatant’s Morale, their morale breaks and they try to surrender or flee in the next Round. Otherwise they keep fighting.

One check per side: Typically a single Morale Check is made for all members of a side, rather than one check per individual.

When to check Morale: The first time a combatant on the same side is killed, and when half of the side has been killed or defeated. For a creature encountered alone, a Morale Check should be made when it is first harmed and when it is reduced to 1/4 or less Hit Points.

A short adventure introducing the perils of Dolmenwood.

Griselma Harrow is a weaver and embroiderer of local renown, possessing the uncanny talent to craft magical garments. She is often commissioned to create such pieces for many luminaries of Dolmenwood, including even the immortal nobles of Fairy.

Recently, she was contacted by Prince Mallowheart, a capricious fairy lord, who demanded she craft him a new coat. Knowing Mallowheart’s cruel nature, Griselma refused. This greatly upset the Prince, and the spiteful lord sent a gang of redcap minions armed with a bag of magic acorns to force her into compliance.

The tricksome redcaps used one of the acorns to sprout an oak tree beneath Griselma’s home, lifting it into the air, and in the chaos they broke inside and captured her. Now, they continue to wreak havoc within the ruined cottage, making it their hideout while their leader Red Tom tries to break Griselma’s will.

The Redcaps

Red Tom: Serious, grumbly voice, one squinty eye. Wears a patched-up, crimson stovepipe hat. The leader of the redcaps, he is single-mindedly focused on the mission and keeps the others in line with the back of his hand.

Glumgrubber: Simple-minded, thick arms. Wears a cherry-red bowler hat cocked to one side. Prefers to settle things with violence. Despite being the largest, he obeys Red Tom unquestioningly.

Knicknocker: Arrogant, scrawny, curled moustache. Wears a scarlet fez. The smallest of the redcaps, he uses his keen intellect to make up for his size. He is bullied by the others, and silently resents them.

Hobnob: Playful, toothy smile. Wears a red-and-pink striped sock hat. Has a love of jokes and pranks, and is easily distracted. Hobnob has grown bored of this job and the mortal world, and just wants something interesting to happen.

Redcap Tactics

If characters make a lot of noise, there is a 2-in-6 chance a nearby redcap will come to investigate. In combat, a redcap fights alone until reduced to half Hit Points, at which point he tries to flee or call for backup if any others are nearby.

If the redcaps successfully knock out any of the Player Characters, they strip them of their valuables and bring them to @UUID[JournalEntry.BbGTV9re1UrfASrM.JournalEntryPage.GYhlIh7BVSpSWtTY]{Area 13} to be tied up with Griselma. If all the Player Characters are knocked out, they awake somewhere in the nearby forest 6 Turns later, stripped of any armour, weapons, and equipment—with embarrassing pictures drawn on their faces.

Redcap

Fairy bandits who enter Dolmenwood at the behest of Prince Mallowheart to taunt, beat, and rob mortals. Look like squat humans with white hair, woolly beards, glinting eyes, and leering grins.

Medium Fairy—Sentient—Chaotic

Level 2 AC 14 HP [[/r 2d8]] (9) Saves D12 R13 H14 B15 S16

Att 2 cudgels (+1, [[/r 1d4]] + knock-out) or nursery rhyme (sleep) Speed 30 Morale 9 XP 35

Cold iron: As fairies, redcaps suffer 1 extra point of damage when hit with cold iron weapons.

Knock-out: Redcaps never fight to kill, but only to knock their foes unconscious. A blow that would reduce the target to 0 HP instead renders it unconscious for 6 Turns, remaining at 1 HP.

Nursery rhymes (once a day): A group of 4 or more redcaps can chant a taunting nursery rhyme that causes [[/r 1d6]] mortals within 50′ to fall into an enchanted sleep for 6 Turns (Save Vs Spell to resist).

Robbery: Unconscious victims are robbed of their possessions (save silver) and sometimes outerwear.

Concerned by reports of bandits prowling the region, the characters travel to Griselma’s woodland cottage only to find things not at all as they had anticipated. A verdant glade in the woods. A 60′ tall oak tree rises from soft, churned earth. Nearby trees are festooned with tangles of coloured yarn. Three sheep lazily amble around the area, chewing on grass. A thatched cottage is stuck in the tree’s canopy, 40′ up, and a rope ladder hangs down from a nearby branch, where a small person (Hobnob) sits. A thick covering of ivy winds its way up the back of the tree trunk, leading up towards the cottage.

Sheep: Each has a notched ear and does not shy away if approached.

Rope ladder: Placed here by the redcaps, leads to @UUID[JournalEntry.BbGTV9re1UrfASrM.JournalEntryPage.t1EwbPrJ9IpXDAF4]{Area 2}. Can be climbed without risk.

Climbing in the Oak

In relaxed circumstances, characters can climb the tree without risk. Pressured circumstances require the Climb Wall skill (no roll required), climbing equipment (rope, grappling hooks), or a Dexterity Check. If the check fails, the character falls.

Combat in the branches: Combatants hit with a successful attack must Save Versus Hold or fall.

Pushing: Characters can attempt to push others out of the tree: make an Attack Roll at a –4 penalty. If the attack succeeds, the target must Save Versus Hold or fall.

Falling: Falling to the ground inflicts [[/r 2d6]] damage.

A thick, sturdy bough stretches out from the cottage window (@UUID[JournalEntry.BbGTV9re1UrfASrM.JournalEntryPage.SW5jE5kXuICIqHCu]{Area 5}). A redcap (Hobnob) sits at the far end, shooting at squirrels with a slingshot and laughing as he sends them tumbling down through the branches.

Hobnob: @UUID[Actor.K6dFhHoAjbMvUG0Q]{Stats}, HP 9. Currently preoccupied with his squirrel shooting. Characters have a 3-in-6 chance to surprise him if approaching quietly.

  • If combat occurs: Hobnob keeps his distance and attacks with his slingshot (missile attack, range 40′, damage [[/r 1d3]]).

Surveying: A character who takes time to observe the nest before approaching will see the circling filchcroupes and is not surprised.

A cosy house with whitewashed, timbered walls and a thatched roof. Unless otherwise stated, all areas are lit by natural light during the day.

Front door: Hangs from one hinge, creakily swinging in the breeze.

Random Happenings

There is a 1-in-6 chance per Turn of a happening occurring while characters are inside the cottage.

Should all 4 assemble, they attempt a nursery rhyme (see @UUID[JournalEntry.BbGTV9re1UrfASrM.JournalEntryPage.keKzdM7mTyOJ3uW5]{Redcap}). In combat, Tom tries to position Griselma between himself and the party.
  • Possessions: 3 gaudy gold rings (25gp each) and a small drawstring bag holding 3 Magic Acorns (see sidebar).

Sack: Contains the redcaps’ loot:

  • Gold: 500gp (fairy coins stamped with the face of Prince Mallowheart).
  • Stolen jewellery: A golden buckle shaped like a coiling wyrm (100gp) and a gilded hand mirror engraved with dancing unicorns (250gp). These were robbed from representatives of the human noble House Guillefer. If returned safely, the house rewards the Player Characters with 300gp.

Griselma Harrow

An elderly human woman with squinting eyes and a wrinkly frown. Her long, grey braid of hair brushes the floor. She wears a sheepskin waistcoat and a woollen dress embroidered with detailed floral patterns and brandishes a knobbled walking cane.

Demeanour (Lawful): Crotchety, headstrong, and quick-witted, but with a softer side she seldom reveals. Tugs at her hair while thinking.

Speech: Shrill and precise. Woldish.

Desires: To expel the “little devils” who captured her. To fix up her house and get it out of this tree.

Medium Mortal—Sentient—Lawful

Level 1 AC 10 HP 4 Saves D12 R13 H14 B15 S16

Att Cane (+0, [[/r 1d3]]) Speed 30 Morale 10 XP 10

Magic Acorn

A fat green acorn with an iridescent cap. When thrown at the ground, it instantly grows into a 60′ tall oak tree.

By defeating the redcaps, the Player Characters are sure to have attracted the ire of Prince Mallowheart, who may meddle in their future endeavours.

If Griselma is rescued and the redcaps dispatched, she gifts the party her Hearty Companion Cloak (see @UUID[JournalEntry.BbGTV9re1UrfASrM.JournalEntryPage.E9TK3FFjqieU46EH]{Area 6}) as thanks. She can also finally tell the characters her job offer: her grandson, Arda Vague, has gone missing, seemingly kidnapped by fairies while visiting the ruins atop the nearby Droomen Knoll (see the Pipes on Droomen Knoll adventure in the Dolmenwood Campaign Book). Alternatively, the Referee may devise their own job or quest hook.

Griselma can also act as a quest-giver for future adventures, if players wish to commission her to make magical garments. She might send them on adventures to collect the rare and magical materials required to make them.

XP For Magic Items (Optional Rule)

The Dolmenwood Campaign Book details several additional options for awarding XP, including milestone awards, XP for spending treasure, exploration awards, and XP for magic items.

If awarding XP for magic items, the values of the items in this adventure are as follows:

  • Hearty Companion Cloak: 8,000gp / 1,600 XP.
  • Jars of magic dye: 200gp / 40 XP each.
  • Magic acorns: 250gp / 50 XP each.

background.notes:
You fled the care of your father—a wicked and infamous knight—to become an acolyte of the Holy Order of St Faxis. You now travel wild lands, bent on aiding the needy, slaying monsters, and sampling the local ales, while you’re at it.

Scented pillow: Lavender. Embroidered with black roses and thorns.

Traits

Combat training: Any armour. Shields. Any weapons.

Decisiveness: Act first on tied Initiative Rolls (humans are treated as the winning side this Round).

Detect holy items: Touching an item for 1 Turn, you can identify whether it is enchanted with holy magic.

Magic armaments: Your holy order forbids you from using magic weapons, armour, and shields of arcane or fairy origin. You may only use holy magic armaments.

Turning the undead: Once a Turn, you can present your holy symbol and attempt to repel undead monsters.

Tiny items: Wooden holy symbol. Frilly shirts and posies. Backpack.

You spent 10 years as a hermit in a cave, struggling over an old prayer book, before concluding that you didn’t really believe in God. Returning to your family, you found your hamlet razed and took up the life of a wandering sell-sword.

Clay effigy: Whispers to you in your sleep.

Traits

Combat training: Any armour. Shields. Any weapons.

Decisiveness: Act first on tied Initiative Rolls (humans are treated as the winning side this Round).

Tiny items: Long sheepskin coat. Backpack.

Orphaned as a child, you grew up scrubbing mugs in the Refuge of St Keye. As an adult, you swore yourself to the life of a wandering friar, aiming to explore all of Dolmenwood, catalogue its profusion of weird fungi, and converse with fairies.

Traits

Combat training: No armour. Club, dagger, staff, sling.

Armour of faith: +2 AC bonus.

Culinary implements: Attack with culinary implements (e.g. frying pan, cured sausage, ham shank) for 1d4 damage.

Decisiveness: Act first on tied Initiative Rolls (humans are treated as the winning side this Round).

Herbalism: Each dose of herbs you administer treats 2 people.

Holy magic: Cast one holy spell per day.

Turning the undead: Once a Turn, you can present your holy symbol and attempt to repel undead monsters.

Tiny items: Friar's habit. Wooden holy symbol. Backpack.

background.notes:
Apprenticed to Lord Malbleat’s wicked sorcerers in the hamlet of Shagsend, you escaped into the night after swindling your masters out of their coin in a drunken game of craps. You since wear your hood low around other breggles.

Tin whistle: Its tones drive cats wild.

Traits

Combat training: No armour. Dagger, staff.

Arcane magic: You can study a spell from your spell book each morning. You can cast it once. Choose one of the arcane spells on p6.

Fur: +1 AC when unarmoured or wearing Light armour.

Horns: You can attack with your horns for 1d4 damage, instead of attacking with a weapon.

Tiny items: Black robes, ostentatiously embroidered with arcane sigils. Huge, hairy overcoat and hood. Backpack.

system.description: For 2 Turns, any script you pass your hand over glows and transforms into the common Woldish tongue. Transformed script reverts when the spell ends.

When cast, choose to either ignite or extinguish:

Ignite: A stream of sparks shoots at a target within 30′, either igniting a light source or inflicting 1 damage (the target may Save Versus Ray to avoid).

Extinguish: Whirling zephyrs snuff out a flame (up to the size of a torch) within 30′. If the flame is held by a creature, they may Save Versus Spell to resist.

A glowing shard of vividly coloured crystal orbits your head for 2 Turns. At any time you can command it to shoot at a target within 120′. It hits unerringly (no Attack Roll or Saving Throw) and inflicts [[/r 1d6+1]] damage. Once fired, the shard is destroyed.

background.notes:
Exiled from your native realm of Fairy for betraying your liege, the enigmatic Duke Who Cherishes Dreams, you wander the mortal world. You have discovered one pleasure in Dolmenwood: breaking mortals’ hearts.

Wine bottle: Empty. When held over a liquid, it draws it inside until full.

Traits

Combat training: Light armour. Small / Medium weapons.

Back-stab: When attacking an unaware target from behind with a dagger: +4 Attack, 3d4 damage on a successful hit.

Vulnerable to cold iron: You suffer 1 extra damage from attacks with cold iron weapons.

Disguise object (glamour): You can magically cause a touched object to appear as something else of similar dimensions. The glamour lasts until someone else touches the object or you use this glamour on a different object.

Unearthly beauty: +2 Charisma (to a maximum of 18) when interacting with mortals.

Tiny items: Decaying regal finery. Backpack.

You were raised by puffball farmers in the sodden reaches of Mulchgrove. Visiting a mould-oracle, you had a vision of becoming a rich tavern owner, brewing your own specialist yeast liqueur. You left your village to find your fortune.

Knobbler: A merriman (miniature, golden swine with curly tusks and twisty tail). Small Animal, Animal Int, Neutral. Level 1, AC 13, HP 4, Saves D12 R13 H14 B15 S16, Att Tusks (+0, 1d4), Speed 40, Morale 7

Traits

Combat training: Light armour. Shields. Any weapons.

Missiles: +1 Attack with all missiles.

Animal companion: Knobbler, see other notes. Follows you everywhere and obeys your basic commands. Never checks Morale if defending you.

Lock singer: 2-in-6 chance of opening a lock by singing to it for 1 Turn.

Resilience: +4 bonus to Saving Throws versus fungal spores and poisons, +2 bonus to all other Saves.

Trophies: When carrying a sizeable trophy from a creature you hunted and killed, you gain a +1 bonus to Attack Rolls and Saving Throws versus creatures of the same type.

Wayfinding: 3-in-6 chance of finding the way again if the party gets lost.

Tiny items: Puffball hat. Backpack.
